''Ampelopsis quinquefolia'' [[André Michaux|Michx.]] }} '''''Parthenocissus quinquefolia''''', commonly known as '''Virginia creeper''', '''woodbine''', '''five-leaved ivy''', or '''five-finger''', is a species of [[flowering plant|flowering]] [[vine]] in the grape family [[Vitaceae]]. The species is [[native plant|native]] to eastern and central [[North America]], with its range extending from south-eastern [[Canada]] and the eastern [[United States]], west to [[Manitoba]] and [[Utah]], and as far south as eastern [[Mexico]] and [[Guatemala]]. It has been introduced globally and is considered an [[invasive species]] to varying degrees in the [[European Union]], the [[United Kingdom]], [[China]], [[Australia]], and [[Cuba]].{{Cite journal |last=Rojas-Sandoval |first=J |date=2017-12-17 |title=Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia creeper) |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.1079/cabicompendium.44676 |journal=CABI Compendium |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=44676 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.44676|doi-access=free }} ==Names== The genus name, ''Parthenocissus'', is a [[Latinisation of names|Latinisation]] of the [[Greek language|Greek]] παρθένος (''parthénos'', "virgin, maiden") + κισσός (''kissós'', "ivy"). The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]], ''quinquefolia'', derives from the [[Latin]] ''quinque'' ("five") + ''folia'' ("leaf"), referring to the leaflets on each compound (palmate) leaf.Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback). pp 292, 324{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 |location=United Kingdom |pages=224}} The name '''Virginia creeper''', referring to both the plant's "virgin" epithet and to part of its native range in the U.S. state of [[Virginia]], is also used for the whole [[genus]] ''[[Parthenocissus]]'', as well as for other species within the genus.{{cite book |last=Coombes |first=Allen J. |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312 |title=The A to Z of plant names |publisher=Timber Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-60469-196-2 |location=USA |pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781604691962/page/312 312] |url-access=registration}} This plant is also known as '''woodbine''' in North America,{{cite book |last=Kenny |first=Hamill |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015009099824;view=1up;seq=714;size=125 |title=West Virginia Place Names: Their Origin and Meaning, Including the Nomenclature of the Streams and Mountains |publisher=The Place Name Press |year=1945 |location=Piedmont, WV |page=690}} although the term can refer to [[Woodbine (plant)|other plant species]]. Other names, such as '''five-leaved ivy''' and '''five-finger''', refer to the leaves' characteristic palmately compound structure. ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' has long been familiar to [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|indigenous peoples in the Americas]]. In the [[Mohawk language]], the plant is called '''kontiráthens'''. In the [[Ojibwe language]], it is called '''mnidoo-biimaakwad bebaamooded'''. The French, who would have encountered the plant by the seventeenth century, gave it the name '''vigne vierge''' ("virgin vine").{{Cite web |title=Virginia Creeper {{!}} Greenbelt Indigenous Botanical Survey |url=https://gibsurvey.ca/species/virginia-creeper |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=gibsurvey.ca}} ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' is not closely related to the true ivy (genus ''[[Hedera]]''), but instead to other members of the [[Vitaceae]] family, including the [[Vitis|grapevine]]. ==Description== [[File:Parthenocissus quinquefolia foliage.jpg|thumb|left|Leaves]] ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' is a prolific [[deciduous]] climber, reaching heights of {{convert|20|-|30|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}} in the wild. It climbs smooth surfaces using small forked [[tendril]]s tipped with small strongly adhesive pads {{convert|5|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=on}} in size.{{Cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=PAQU2|title=USDA Plants Database: Parthenocissus quinquefolia (L.) Planch. Virginia creeper|website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]|access-date=July 30, 2021}} ===Leaves=== The leaves are [[Leaf#Divisions of the blade|palmately compound]], composed of five leaflets (rarely three leaflets, particularly on younger vines, and sometimes seven) joined from a central point on the leafstalk, and range from {{convert|3|to|20|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} (rarely to {{convert|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on|disp=or}}) across. The leaflets have a toothed margin. Seedlings have heart-shaped [[cotyledon]] leaves. The species is often confused with ''[[Parthenocissus vitacea|P. vitacea]]'' or "False Virginia creeper", which has the same leaves, but does not have the adhesive pads at the end of its tendrils. It is sometimes mistaken for ''[[Toxicodendron radicans]]'' (poison ivy), despite having five leaflets (poison ivy has three).{{Cite NSRW|wstitle=Virginia Creeper}} While the leaves of ''P. quinquefolia'' do not produce [[urushiol]], the sap within the leaves and stem contains [[raphides]] (needle-shaped crystals of [[calcium oxalate]]) which can puncture the skin causing irritation and blisters similar to poison ivy in sensitive people. The reactions are generally less severe than those of poison ivy.{{Cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_paqu2.pdf|title=Plant Guide: VIRGINIA CREEPER Parthenocissus quinquefolia |website=[[United States Department of Agriculture]]|access-date=July 30, 2021}} The leaves sometimes turn a decorative bright red in the fall. ===Flowers and berries=== The flowers are small and greenish, produced in inconspicuous clusters in late spring, and mature in late summer or early fall into small hard purplish-black berries {{convert|5|to|7|mm|in|frac=16|abbr=on}} diameter. These berries contain toxic amounts of [[oxalic acid]] and have been known to cause kidney damage and death to humans.{{cite book|last1=Tull|first1=Delena|title=Edible and useful plants of the Southwest|date=2013|isbn=978-0-292-74827-9|pages=184–185|edition=Revised|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GdmGAAAAQBAJ&q=Parthenocissus+quinquefolia+concentration+of+oxalic+acid&pg=PA184}}{{cite web |url=http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=28740 |title=FDA Poisonous Plant Database |website=[[Food and Drug Administration]] |access-date= October 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140911170909/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/detail.cfm?id=28740|archive-date=September 11, 2014}} The berries are not toxic to birds and provide an important winter food source for many bird species. ==Cultivation and uses== [[Image:Parthenocissus quinquefolia, hegwortels, Manie van der Schijff BT, a.jpg|upright=0.68|thumb|right|Climbing roots with adhesive pads, which are absent in ''[[Parthenocissus vitacea|P. vitacea]]'']] ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]], because of its ability to rapidly cover walls and buildings, and its deep red to [[Burgundy (color)|burgundy]] fall (autumn) foliage.{{cite web|url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/virginia-creeper-parthenocissus-quinquefolia/|title=Virginia Creeper, Parthenocissus quinquefolia|website=Wisconsin Horticulture}} It can easily be propagated by stem [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]] taken in spring.[https://www.thespruce.com/taxonomy-of-virginia-creeper-2132897#:~:text=To%20propagate%20Virginia%20creeper%20from,at%20least%203%20inches%20deep. How to Grow and Care for Virginia Creeper] [[Dotdash Meredith|The Spruce]] It is frequently seen covering telephone poles or trees. It may kill other plants it covers by shading its support and thus limiting the supporting plants' ability to [[photosynthesis|photosynthesize]]. With its aggressive growth, it can overburden slower-growing understory trees with its weight, damaging them. Its ability to propagate via its extensive root system makes it difficult to eradicate.{{cite web|last=Tilton|first=Lois|date=March 13, 2013|title=The Invaders: Virginia Creeper|url=https://www.davesgarden.com/guides/articles/|access-date=September 25, 2021|website=www.davesgarden.com}}{{Cite web|title=Virginia Creeper: Ornamental or Nuisance?|url=https://www.anokamastergardeners.org/blog/2016/4/6/virginia-creeper-ornamental-or-nuisance|access-date=September 25, 2021|website=Anoka County Master Gardeners|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210925114540/https://www.anokamastergardeners.org/blog/2016/4/6/virginia-creeper-ornamental-or-nuisance|archive-date=September 25, 2021}} ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' can be used as a shading vine for buildings on masonry walls. Because the vine, like its relative ''[[Parthenocissus tricuspidata|P. tricuspidata]]'' (Boston ivy), adheres to the surface by disks rather than penetrating roots, it does not harm the masonry but will keep a building cooler by shading the wall surface during the summer. As with ivy, ripping the plant from the wall will leave the adhesive disks behind. If the plant clings to fragile surfaces it can first be killed by severing the vine from the root. The adhesive pads will then eventually deteriorate and release their grip. The plant should be trimmed regularly to keep it from growing into areas where it is not wanted. If allowed to penetrate into the wall of a frame house, it will grow upward within the wall until it finds a place to emerge.{{Cite web|url=https://www.fassadengruen.de/en/building-damages.html|title=Facade Greening: Damage caused by Ivy and other Climbing Plants to Buildings|website=www.fassadengruen.de}}{{cite web|url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/parthenocissus-quinquefolia|title=Parthenocissus quinquefolia (Virginia Creeper)|website=Gardenia.net|access-date=August 19, 2024}} == Invasive status == Initially cultivated as an ornamental, ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' escaped from gardens to become naturalized and invasive around the globe. According to the [[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]], as of 2025, the plant has become established on all continents except Antarctica.{{Cite web |title=Parthenocissus Planch. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3039188 |access-date=2025-06-02 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}} In the United Kingdom, ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' is listed on Schedule 9 of the [[Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981]] as an invasive non-native species. While this does not prevent it from being sold in the UK, or from being grown in gardens, the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] (RHS) encourages those who grow it to take great care with managing it and with disposing of unwanted material. The RHS also encourages gardeners to find alternative plants to grow to those listed on Schedule 9.{{Cite web |title=Invasive non-native plants |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/garden-health/weeds/Invasive-non-native-species |access-date=July 30, 2021 |website=[[Royal Horticultural Society]]}} ''Parthenocissus quinquefolia'' is listed as an environmental weed in Australia.{{Cite web |title=Fact sheet Index |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/index.htm |access-date=2025-06-02 |website=keyserver.lucidcentral.org}} It is also listed as an invasive species in several countries in Europe, China, and Cuba. In 2024, the plant (along with the closely related ''[[Parthenocissus inserta|P. inserta]]'') was listed as an invasive alien in [[Switzerland]], which banned its sale, gifting, renting, and import.{{Cite web |title=Fedlex |url=https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2008/614/en |access-date=2025-06-02 |website=www.fedlex.admin.ch}} ==See also== * ''[[Parthenocissus inserta|P. inserta]]'' or ''P. vitacea'', thicket creeper or false Virginia creeper * ''[[Parthenocissus tricuspidata|P. tricuspidata]]'' or ''Ampelopsis veitchii'', Boston ivy or Japanese creeper ==Gallery== Image:Parthenocissus quinquefolia20110704 003.jpg|Flower Image:Parthenocissus quinquefolia on wall, November 1, 2008.jpg|Berries after the leaves have dropped in autumn File:Parthenocissus quinquefolia seedling.jpg|Seedling with heart-shaped cotyledon leaves Image:Parthenocissus_quinquefolia_Leaf.jpg|Emerging leaf in spring File:TreeVine.JPG|Thick vine File:Virginiacreepertendril.jpg|Tendrils beginning to twine around a metal trellis File:Kisus.JPG|Fall color Image:6370VirginiaCreeper.jpg|Fall color Cissus sicyoides.JPG|Climbing a building wall Bad Dürkheim Schlossgartenstraße 2 001 2020 10 20.jpg|Covering a building Parthenocissus quinquefoliar Ireland (2).jpg|Covering a wall Parthenocissus quinquefolia London 1.jpg|Covering a wall in London Marienthal (Ahr) -
